correctness.rationale: The feasible simplices are compact and the objective continuous. For each site 2 phi(c)phi(q)=phi(c)^2+phi(q)^2-(phi(c)-phi(q))^2; with identical normalized budgets each square sum is bounded by the same scalar maximum. Taking equal vectors attains it, and zero loss requires c_i=q_i at every site by strict monotonicity. For g(x)=x^2/(1+x)^2, g'(x)-g'(y) has sign (x-y)[1-xy(3+x+y)]. On the smaller-dose half of a two-site transfer with sum u, the bracket 1-x(u-x)(3+u) is strictly decreasing, so any stationary point there is a strict minimum, not a maximum. Thus every positive-dose subset is uniform at a global optimum, including optima on the boundary. For k positive sites the score is T^2 k/(T+k)^2; the sign of its adjacent increment is exactly the sign of T^2-k(k+1). The increasing thresholds give the stated unique support size or adjacent two-way tie, with every subset of each winning size attainable. The single-resource contrast follows by strict concavity of phi. The frozen finite checker and notes were inspected, not executed; the proof covers arbitrary real doses and finite n.

value.rationale: Under the stipulated balanced complementarity model, the complete equality cases distinguish when adding a hotspot beats more concentrated supply and force both independently allocable inputs to use the same sites. Closed transition budgets and ties across all n are meaningful for a static benchmark and contrast with strict spreading for one resource. No optimization of growth over time, field recommendation, or unequal-budget extrapolation is justified.
